/workspace.content: # Threat Model — Doggy Player (Electron desktop media player) ## Overview Doggy Player is a Windows desktop video player built with **Electron + React (Vite)**. Two source trees are in scope: - `src/` — React renderer (`App.tsx` ~279KB monolith, `ContextMenu.tsx`, `main.tsx`, `index.css`). Runs **inside the Electron renderer process**. - `electron/` — main process (`main.js` ~45KB), usage telemetry/gating module (`telemetry.js`), and a separate stats window document (`usage-stats.html`). There is **no server-side component and no backend API owned by this project** except an external counter service (`https://abacus.jasoncameron.dev`) used for anonymous install-count telemetry. Product surfaces (in-scope, production): 1. Renderer UI (local `dist/index.html` in packaged builds, `http://127.0.0.1:3000` in dev). 2. Main-process IPC handlers: `quit-app`, `restart-and-install`, `iptv-fetch`, `get-network-info`, `get-stream-url`, `cancel-seek-optimize`, `probe-seek-quality`, `optimize-for-seeking`, `extract-seek-frame`, plus telemetry IPC (`telemetry:get/set`, `creator-stats:login/load`). 3. Local Express media server bound to `127.0.0.1:` serving `/stream?path=&token=` — file streaming and ffmpeg transcode/remux. 4. IPTV / remote VOD playback (attacker-influenced remote HTTP responses are consumed into both the renderer DOM and ffmpeg). 5. Auto-updater (packaged only) and a gated "creator stats" window reachable via `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D`. Non-production / not in scope as findings: `vite-env.d.ts`, build tooling, and any local dev-only code path that cannot ship to users. ## Trust Boundaries and Assumptions **Critically, the renderer is NOT a sandboxed boundary.** `createWindow()` (`electron/main.js:568-580`) sets: ```js webPreferences: { nodeIntegration: true, contextIsolation: false, webSecurity: false } ``` So anything executing in the renderer has full Node.js and unrestricted filesystem/network access, and can `invoke` every IPC handler. Anything that achieves script execution *in the renderer* is equivalent to full local code execution under the user's account. The stats window has the same posture (`nodeIntegration:true, contextIsolation:false`, `electron/telemetry.js` `openStatsWindow`). Because of this, the meaningful trust boundaries are: - **Attacker-controlled inputs (untrusted):** - IPTV/VOD playlist contents and the remote media/CDN responses (M3U/M3U8/XMLTV, `tvg-*` attributes, channel names, logos, EPG descriptions) — gameable by whoever operates or hijacks the provider. - Remote HTTP responses fetched through the `iptv-fetch` IPC bridge and rendered/parsed by the renderer. - `req.query` on the loopback media server (`path`, `token`, `start`, `transcode`, `vforce`) — reachable from any other local process and potentially from web content launched by the player. - Filenames / paths passed on the command line (`process.argv`), including on `second-instance`. - Remote media file names/extensions/metadata used to build ffmpeg argv and cache paths. - **User-controlled (trusted-ish):** local file selection through the OS file dialog; user toggles (telemetry on/off). - **Developer-controlled (trusted):** hard-coded gate credentials/hashes, update feed URL config, `nodeIntegration` posture. **Invariants that must hold:** - External input must never reach `spawn`/`exec`/`ffmpeg` argv, filesystem paths, or `executeJavaScript` in an unescaped form. - The `iptv-fetch` bridge should not become a general-purpose SSRF primitive against loopback/RFC1918/addressing (`abacus`, routers, Ollama/Mongo/Redis on localhost, cloud metadata endpoints). - The loopback media server must not allow arbitrary file read for a requester that lacks the token, and the token must not leak cross-origin. - The renderer must not be navigable to attacker-controlled origins while carrying `nodeIntegration` — a single navigation to an attacker page yields RCE. - `webSecurity:false` means cross-origin reads succeed inside the renderer; combined with `iptv-fetch` this is a two-way door into the LAN. ## Attack Surface and Attacker Stories **Exposed surfaces:** - `ipcMain.handle('iptv-fetch')` — takes a fully attacker-influenced `url` and forwards `options.headers`/`options.body` to `fetch`. No scheme allowlist, no private-range blocking, no redirect policy, and it returns the response body to the renderer. This is a textbook desktop-app SSRF and is the highest-value target on this scan. - `ipcMain.handle('get-stream-url' | 'extract-seek-frame' | 'probe-seek-quality' | 'optimize-for-seeking')` — accept a `filePath` from the renderer, which under `nodeIntegration:true` can originate from remote playlist metadata. All flow into `resolveLocalMediaPath()` (no normalization/containment) → `spawn(ffmpeg, [...])` and `fs.createReadStream`. - `req.query.path` on the loopback `/stream` server — the `token` guard is the only control; verify whether the token can leak (Referer to a remote host during IPTV playback is the likely vector) and what happens after a leak. - Renderer rendering of remote playlist/EPG data into the DOM (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `innerHTML`, data URIs, `` from playlist logos) — under `nodeIntegration` this escalates quickly. - `executeJavaScript` calls in `main.js` on `did-finish-load` / `second-instance` building `window.__initialVideoInfo = ${JSON.stringify(fileArg)}` — check JSON-escaping sufficiency for ``/U+2028 style breakouts. - Remote URL handling in `get-stream-url` returning `redirect(videoPath)` and building ffmpeg input from a remote URL. - `usage-stats.html` innerHTML templating with `row.date`/`row.count` from the counter service — remote data into HTML in a `nodeIntegration` window. - Gated creator-stats login (`telemetry.js`) — SHA-256 password hashes in source, client-side gate with `statsAuthed` boolean. - Auto-updater signature/feed trust in packaged mode. - `spawn('powershell.exe', [...])` priority helper interpolating a PID (verify the PID source is genuinely numeric). **Not realistic here:** multi-tenant or cross-user authorization issues (single-user desktop app), CSRF against a web server, server-side SQLi/XXE (no backend), and any attack requiring the attacker to already have local shell access — though note that a local attacker's ability to reach the loopback stream server with a leaked token *is* meaningful because it is reachable from a browser context. ## Severity Calibration - **Critical** — attacker-controlled code execution in the renderer/main process reachable from ordinary product use (e.g. a malicious IPTV playlist or a compromised provider response leading to RCE), or an unauthenticated network attacker reaching local files. - **High** — an unauthenticated/local-web-content path to arbitrary local file read, an SSRF that demonstrably reaches loopback or RFC1918 services with response data returned to the attacker, or remote feed compromise of the update channel. - **Medium** — SSRF that is real but constrained (e.g. only from an already-compromised renderer), sensitive-token leakage requiring a specific interaction, stored/reflected injection limited to the local user's own UI without escalation. - **Low / Info** — hard-coded gate credentials protecting only a vanity statistics panel, missing CSP in a `file://` doc, verbose logging, dependency hygiene. Because the renderer already holds Node privileges by design, findings should be scored by **who can reach the renderer input** (remote playlist provider vs. a local process vs. the user themself), not by "the renderer could execute code anyway".
